title: Aggregate Functions
description: Summarize your data with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. Learn how aggregate functions work with and without GROUP BY.

data.text: Aggregate functions take many rows as input and return a single value. They are the foundation of any analytical query — how many orders did we get? What is the average sale? What was our best month?

data.title: Different ways to count
COUNT(*) vs. COUNT(column)
data.text: COUNT(*) counts every row, including those where a column is NULL. COUNT(column) skips NULL values. If you want to know 'how many rows have a value in this field?', use COUNT(column).

data.title: Revenue and average order value
data.code:
SELECT
    COUNT(order_id)              AS total_orders,
    SUM(quantity * list_price)
                                 AS total_revenue,
    AVG(quantity * list_price)
                                 AS avg_order_value
FROM   sales.orders o
INNER JOIN sales.order_items i
    ON i.order_id = o.order_id;

data.text: MIN and MAX work not just on numbers — they return the 'smallest' and 'largest' value for any comparable type, including strings and dates.

data.title: Min/Max on strings and dates
data.code:
-- Alphabetically first and last product name
SELECT MIN(product_name) AS first_product,
       MAX(product_name) AS last_product
FROM   production.products;

-- First and last order date
SELECT MIN(order_date) AS first_order,
       MAX(order_date) AS last_order
FROM   sales.orders;

data.text: When you use an aggregate function without a GROUP BY clause, the entire result set collapses into a single row. This is useful for grand totals and overall summaries.

data.title: Overall summary of all orders
data.code:
SELECT
    COUNT(*)             AS total_orders,
    SUM(quantity * list_price * (1 - discount)) AS total_revenue,
    AVG(list_price)      AS avg_product_price,
    MIN(list_price)      AS cheapest_product,
    MAX(list_price)      AS most_expensive_product
FROM   sales.order_items;

data.title: Mixing aggregates and plain columns
data.text: If you use an aggregate function alongside a non-aggregated column in the same SELECT, SQL Server requires that the non-aggregated columns appear in a GROUP BY clause. Otherwise you get an error.

data.title: Rich summary report
data.code:
SELECT
    COUNT(DISTINCT category_id) AS categories,
    COUNT(DISTINCT brand_id)    AS brands,
    AVG(list_price)             AS avg_price,
    MIN(list_price)             AS min_price,
    MAX(list_price)             AS max_price
FROM   production.products;

data.title: Aggregate essentials
points: COUNT(*), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX collapse many rows into one value
COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values
Aggregates skip NULLs — except COUNT(*) which counts rows
Without GROUP BY, the whole table becomes one summary row
Mixing aggregates with plain columns requires GROUP BY
